extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, and magistrates studying English common law (Blackstone's Commentaries)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the offices, powers, qualifications, duties, and tenure of local magistrates and officers in English common law (justices of the peace, constables, surveyors of highways, overseers of the poor), and rules for settlement and allegiance. Includes statutory rules, procedural requirements, and customary practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of justices by royal commission under the great seal
rubrics_metrics.description: These justices are appointed by the king's special commission under the great seal; the form of which was settled A.D. 1590. The commission appoints them jointly and severally to keep the peace, and authorises any two or more to enquire of and determine felonies and misdemeanors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commission commonly names particular persons to be always included (quorum clause, "quorum aliquem vestrum... unum esse volumus"), whence the persons named are called justices of the quorum. Formerly only a select number were of the quorum; modern practice often names nearly all. No business is to be done without the presence of certain particular justices when so directed by the commission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quorum clause and practice (justices of the quorum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The commission frequently directs that some particular justices or one of them be always included; persons so named are called justices of the quorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically a select number only were of the quorum; modern practice tends to include most justices by naming them again in the quorum clause. Statute 26 Geo. II. c. 27: no exception is allowable for not expressing in warrants etc. that the justice who issued them is of the quorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of justices (statutory history)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute provisions have prescribed numbers for keepers of the peace/justices: e.g., 18 Edw. III. c. 2. ordained two or three; 34 Edw. III. c. 1. provided one lord and three or four worthy men (with some learned in law); later statutes restrained numbers to six or eight but practice grew larger again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The growth in statute business has reasonably occasioned an increase in number beyond the medieval limits; historical statutes show fluctuating numerical limits but modern practice disregards strict caps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications of justices (reputation, rank, residence, property, disqualifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes direct justices to be of the best reputation and most worthy men in the county; 13 Ric. II. c. 10. orders them to be sufficient knights, esquires, and gentlemen of the law; residency in their counties is required (2 Hen. V.). Property qualification originally 20_l. per annum (18 Hen. VI. c. 11.), updated to 100_l. per annum clear (5 Geo. II. c. 11.), with oath to be made of this qualification. Practising attorneys, solicitors, or proctors are disqualified (5 Geo. II.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a justice acts without the required qualification he shall forfeit 100_l. The property qualification and oath are intended to prevent appointment of men of small substance whose poverty makes them covetous and contemptible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure and modes of determination of the office of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The office subsists only during the king's pleasure and is determinable 1) by the demise of the crown (in six months), 2) by express writ under the great seal discharging a person, 3) by supersedeas which suspends commissions, 4) by a new commission that omits former justices (two commissions cannot subsist), and 5) by accession of the office of sheriff or coroner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Former thought that acquiring a new dignity determined the office, but statute (1 Edw. VI. c. 7.) provides that notwithstanding a new title the justice shall still continue a justice in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers and duties of a single justice vs. two or more
rubrics_metrics.description: A single justice is empowered to conserve the peace (suppress riots and affrays, take securities for the peace, apprehend and commit felons and inferior criminals). Any two or more justices are empowered to hear and determine all felonies and other offences (ground of jurisdiction at sessions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The powers of justices arise from their commission and the numerous statutes conferring jurisdiction; the accumulation of business has made the office extensive and complicated. The text recommends lenity for undesigned slips by well-meaning justices and notes statutory protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protections and liabilities of justices in discharge of office
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes protect justices from suits for oversights without prior notice and allow suits to be stopped when sufficient amends are tendered; malicious or tyrannical abuse is severely punished and persons who recover verdicts against a justice for wilful or malicious injury are entitled to double costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These protections are designed to enable upright discharge of troublesome duties while deterring willful misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form, origin, and duties of constables (high and petty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constables (derived from comes stabuli) are officers appointed for keeping the peace and regulating arms and armour; statute of Winchester directs two constables in every hundred and franchise to inspect matters relating to arms and armour. There are high constables (appointed at court leets or quarter sessions) and petty constables (inferior officers in towns and parishes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petty constables combine an ancient office (headborough/tithing-man) and a more modern constable function instituted about Edward III; they are chosen by jury at the court leet or, if none, appointed by two justices of the peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: General duties and powers of constables
rubrics_metrics.description: Constables must keep the king's peace in their districts; powers include arresting, imprisoning, breaking open houses, appointing watchmen, and other statutory duties. They must keep watch and ward (daytime ward and nighttime watch), enforce gate closures in walled towns from sunset to sunrise, and may appoint deputies (watchmen) who wield their authority temporarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hundreds are answerable for robberies committed within them by day for negligent guard. The statute of Winchester governs much of these duties; many minute duties are spread by various statutes (refer to Lambard and Burn for details).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ward and watch definitions and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Ward (custodia) is chiefly daytime intended to apprehend rioters and robbers; watch pertains to night and begins when ward ends. In walled towns the gates shall be closed from sunsetting to sunrising and watch kept in boroughs and towns to apprehend rogues, vagabonds, and night-walkers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constables may appoint watchmen regulated by the custom of the place; these watchmen, as deputies, have the authority of the constable for the time being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveyors of highways — parish duty and appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: Every parish is bound to keep high roads through it in good and sufficient repair (part of the trinoda necessitas). Where parishes neglected repairs, statute 2 & 3 Ph. & M. c. 8. ordered surveyors of the highways in every parish. Originally appointed by constable and churchwardens, they are now constituted by two neighbouring justices out of substantial inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualifications for surveyors: inhabitants with either 10_l. per annum of their own, or rent 30_l. a year, or personal estate worth 100_l. (statute 3 W. & M. c. 12.). The office corresponds in civil purpose to Roman curatores viarum but with less dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveyors' duties and specific statutory powers for highway repairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveyors must: 1) remove annoyances in highways or give notice to the owner to remove them (penalties for noncompliance); 2) call inhabitants six days a year to labour in repairing highways, requiring teams or workers from persons keeping draughts/occupying lands; 3) ensure work completed before harvest; 4) ensure every cartway be at least eight feet wide (quarter sessions may increase to 24 feet); 5) lay out money to purchase materials if insufficient and be reimbursed by a rate allowed at special sessions; 6) where personal labour is insufficient, may levy a rate (not exceeding 6_d. in the pound) with quarter sessions' consent and must account on oath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turnpike trusts and specific road acts are distinct and depend on particular powers therein; surveyors' powers are statutory and require accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overseers of the poor — appointment and qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute 43 Eliz. c. 2. overseers of the poor are to be nominated yearly in Easter-week or within one month after, by two justices dwelling near the parish. They must be substantial householders and so expressed in the appointment of the justices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their appointment and duties have been further elaborated by subsequent statutes; reference to Raym. for authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overseers' duties — relief and employment of the poor
rubrics_metrics.description: Their principal duties are: first, to raise competent sums for the necessary relief of the poor, impotent, old, blind, and those unable to work; second, to provide work for those able to work (original statute favoured providing stocks to be worked at home rather than common workhouses). They are empowered to make and levy rates upon inhabitants of the parish for these purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticises neglect of employment provision and defends the Elizabethan plan of relieving only the impotent and providing home-based work to preserve domestic connexions and industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: General objectives and policy of Elizabethan poor law
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute of Elizabeth intended two great objects: 1) to relieve the impotent poor (those unable to work), and 2) to find employment for those able to work, principally by providing stocks to be worked at home rather than gathering all poor in a workhouse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary argues this system preserves domestic ties, incentivises honest labour, and prevents equalising wages between industrious and dissolute poor; critiques later changes that made settlement rules more intricate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of acquiring a parish settlement (general heads, ten enumerated methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law reduces acquisition of settlement to general heads: 1) By birth (prima facie); 2) By parentage (settlement of one's parents); 3) By marriage (a woman takes husband's settlement, with qualifications for foreign husbands); 4) By forty days' residence with notice (residence = lodging/lying, not by fraud); 5) By renting for a year a tenement of yearly value of 10_l. and residing 40 days (gains settlement without notice); 6) By being charged to and paying the parish taxes and levies; 7) By executing public parochial office for a whole year (e.g., churchwarden) coupled with 40 days' residence; 8) By being hired for a year when unmarried and serving that year; 9) By being bound apprentice for seven years; 10) By having an estate of one's own and residing there 40 days when estate acquired by descent, gift, or devise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forty days' residence must be accompanied by notice in writing to an overseer (read in church and registered) to count; certain equivalents to notice (payment of taxes, public office) are recognised. Acquiring property by purchase is treated specially: unless bona fide consideration of 30_l. is paid, purchase does not create a permanent settlement beyond the time one inhabits it (stat. 9 Geo. I. c. 7.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificates, removals, and limits on gaining settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a parish grants a certificate acknowledging a person as their parishioner, that person cannot be removed merely because likely to become chargeable but only when actually chargeable. Certificated persons cannot gain settlement by the ordinary means listed (e.g., forty days' residence) except by renting a tenement of 10_l. per annum or serving an annual office while legally placed there. Apprentices or servants to certificated persons cannot gain settlement by their service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two justices of the peace may remove persons not so settled if adjudged likely to become chargeable, except where the person is in the process of gaining a legal settlement (e.g., hired for a year, or renting a qualifying tenement). The law of settlements has many branches by resolutions of the courts and statutory modification over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal process for intruders and those likely to become chargeable
rubrics_metrics.description: All persons not settled may be removed to their own parishes on complaint of the overseers by two justices of the peace if adjudged likely to become chargeable to the parish into which they have intruded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: those in the way of getting a legal settlement (hired for a year, or renting a tenement of 10_l. per annum) are not removable. The courts' resolutions over the preceding century have greatly branched the rules of settlement and removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and forms of allegiance (natural-born vs aliens, oaths)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural-born subjects are those born within the dominions of the crown (within the allegiance); aliens are born out of it. Allegiance is the tie binding subject to king in return for protection. There is an implied, original, and virtual allegiance owing antecedently to any express promise or oath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical oaths (fealty vs allegiance) and forms evolved: ancient oath of allegiance was explicit; at the Revolution a more general oath was adopted; oath of supremacy renounces pope's authority; oath of abjuration (introduced in William's reign) recognizes the king's right, engages to support him, to disclose conspiracies, and renounces the pretender. The oath of allegiance may be tendered to persons above twelve, and the oath of abjuration/supremacy must be taken by persons in office; two justices may tender oaths under statute authority.
